\chapter{Sorry}
\label{ch:ml-sorry}
\hlchaptermodality{9}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can apologise in Malayalam with kṣamikkaṇaṁ, and use the plainer kṣamikkū when it suits.}

Say kṣamikkaṇaṁ, hear the necessitative -aṇaṁ softening it into politeness, then drop to the plain kṣamikkū.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[kṣamikkaṇaṁ]{\ml{ക്ഷമിക്കണം} (kṣamikkaṇaṁ) — (you) should forgive / sorry}

\label{lesson:ML-C09-kshamikkanam}



\begin{quote}
You already know \textbf{\ml{ദയവായി}} and the necessitative \textbf{‑\ml{ണം}} ending mentioned there. Malayalam's \textquotedblleft{}sorry\textquotedblright{} is that very ending, now carrying a forgiveness-verb.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ml{ക്ഷമ}} (\emph{kṣama}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{forgiveness, patience}\textquotedblright{} — the Sanskrit noun.
  \item \textbf{‑\ml{ഇക്കുക}} (\emph{‑ikkuka}) = a \textbf{verb-making suffix}: \emph{kṣama} + \emph{‑ikkuka} $\to$ \textbf{\ml{ക്ഷമിക്കുക}} (\emph{kṣamikkuka}), \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to forgive}.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textbf{‑\ml{ണം}} (\emph{‑aṇaṁ}) = the \textbf{necessitative} ending, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{must / should}\textquotedblright{} — literally \emph{kṣamikkaṇaṁ} says \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{{[}you{]} must forgive},\textquotedblright{} used as a softened, polite request exactly the way English can soften a request into \textquotedblleft{}you should really forgive me\textquotedblright{} without meaning it as an order.
\end{itemize}

So \textbf{\ml{ക്ഷമിക്കണം}} leans on obligation to be polite — a very different move from a plain imperative.

\begin{culture}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Malayalam \textbf{\ml{ക്ഷമിക്കണം}} \emph{kṣami\textbf{kkaṇaṁ}} — Sanskrit \emph{kṣama} + \textbf{‑ikkuka} (verb) + \textbf{‑aṇaṁ} (necessitative: \textquotedblleft{}must/should\textquotedblright{})
  \item Kannada \textbf{\ka{ಕ್ಷಮಿಸಿ}} \emph{kṣami\textbf{si}} — Sanskrit \emph{kṣamā} + \textbf{‑isu} (verb) + \textbf{‑i} (imperative)
  \item Telugu \textbf{\te{క్షమించండి}} \emph{kṣamin̄\textbf{caṇḍi}} — Sanskrit \emph{kṣamā} + \textbf{‑in̄cu} (verb) + \textbf{‑aṇḍi} (imperative)
  \item Tamil \textbf{\ta{மன்னிக்கவும்}} \emph{maṉṉi\textbf{kkavum}} — its \textbf{own} native root \emph{maṉṉi}, not Sanskrit at all
\end{itemize}
\end{culture}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{\ml{ക്ഷമിക്കണം}} is a genuine, common way to ask forgiveness — but Malayalam speakers reach just as often for the plain imperative \textbf{\ml{ക്ഷമിക്കൂ}} (\emph{kṣamikkū}, using the \textbf{‑\ml{ൂ}} ending from the please lesson) or simply the borrowed English \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}sorry.\textquotedblright{}}
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}kṣama\textquotedblright{} — the Sanskrit noun, forgiveness
  \item the verb — \textquotedblleft{}kṣamikkuka,\textquotedblright{} to forgive — then \textquotedblleft{}kṣamikkaṇaṁ,\textquotedblright{} you should forgive
  \item the plainer version — \textquotedblleft{}kṣamikkū,\textquotedblright{} using the ‑ū ending you know
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\ml{ക്ഷമിക്കണം}} literally say, and why is that polite? (\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}{[}You{]} must forgive\textquotedblright{}} — the necessitative \textbf{‑aṇaṁ} softens an obligation into a request, same as \emph{\ml{ദയവായി}}'s note on ‑aṇaṁ.) Which cousins also verb-ify \emph{kṣama}? (\textbf{Kannada and Telugu}; \textbf{Tamil} uses its own root \emph{maṉṉi}.) What's a plainer alternative? (\textbf{Kṣamikkū}, using the ‑ū ending, or borrowed English \textquotedblleft{}sorry.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ā]{\ml{◌ാ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:ML-S04-vowel-sign-aa}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \ml{◌ി} — what does it do?

One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ml{◌ാ}}
\textbf{\ml{◌ാ}} — \emph{ā}.

It is a \textbf{vowel sign}. It is not a letter and never stands alone: it attaches to a consonant and \textbf{replaces} the \emph{a} built into it with \emph{ā}. Replaces, not adds — the \emph{a} is gone.

You already say these, and every one of them has \ml{◌ാ} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ml{നമസ്കാരം}} \emph{namaskāram} — hello / greetings (namaskāram — \textquotedblleft{}a making of a bow\textquotedblright{})
  \item \textbf{\ml{സാരമില്ല}} \emph{sāramilla} — it doesn't matter / no problem / you're welcome
  \item \textbf{\ml{പോയി} \ml{വരാം}} \emph{pōyi varāṁ} — goodbye (lit. \textquotedblleft{}I'll go and come back\textquotedblright{})
  \item \textbf{\ml{നാളെ} \ml{കാണാം}} \emph{nāḷe kāṇāṁ} — see you tomorrow
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \ml{◌ാ} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \ml{◌ാ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \ml{◌ാ} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\ml{നമസ്കാരം}  ·  \ml{സാരമില്ല}  ·  \ml{നന്ദി}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \ml{◌ാ} three times, saying \emph{ā} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \ml{◌ാ} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \ml{◌ാ}? What vowel does it put on the consonant it attaches to — and what does it take off? (\textbf{Puts \emph{ā} on; takes the built-in \emph{a} off.}) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pa]{\ml{പ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:ML-S112-letter-pa}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \ml{ച} — what does it do?

One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ml{പ}}
\textbf{\ml{പ}} — \emph{pa}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{p}, it is \textbf{pa}.

You already say these, and every one of them has \ml{പ} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ml{പേര്}} \emph{pēr} — name
  \item \textbf{\ml{എന്റെ} \ml{പേര്} … \ml{ആണ്}} — my name is…
  \item \textbf{\ml{നിന്റെ} \ml{പേര്} \ml{എന്താണ്}?} — what's your name?
  \item \textbf{\ml{പോയി} \ml{വരാം}} \emph{pōyi varāṁ} — goodbye (lit. \textquotedblleft{}I'll go and come back\textquotedblright{})
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \ml{പ} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \ml{പ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \ml{പ} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\ml{പേര്}  ·  \ml{നമസ്കാരം}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \ml{പ} three times, saying \emph{pa} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \ml{പ} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \ml{പ}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{pa}}.) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
